units.translation: the blessed gods who rule the city
the land neighboring upon the Ethiopians
may I never see this city stormed
But of the glorious contests of the slain in battle I will not endure not to honor this city as victorious among mortals.
and of all the gods who protect the city, the highest, the nether
free and unplundered, with inviolability from mortals
Thus I wrote instead of καρπὸς οὐ κομιστέος [fruit not to be gathered], which is the work of an interpolator filling a lacuna.]
There is nothing worse than bad company, whose fruit is unprofitable.
so that without a quiver I may close this eye
and security for those who walk through the city
from which verse ἀσφαλέας [safe] (ἀσφαλείας [security] first hand of M) was introduced into verse 148 by a scribe who strayed from the previous verse.
For when men are alive, it is a sure bulwark.
But how might we share in safe counsels?
and it falls not safely even on its back
the daughter of Zeus, holding holy things before her face, most secure (thus I corrected for ασφαλές [secure])

explained by ἀκατάστατον [unstable] in Etym. M. p. 161, 15 from Aeschylus (fr. 363). Explained by ἀμετάσχετον [not to be shared] in Hesychius, where Schrevelius corrected to ἀκατάσχετον [unrestrainable], which Nauck also restored in Etym. M. for ἀκατάστατον [unstable].

Thus Herwerden for άσχαλᾷ [he is distressed], just as L. Dindorf restored ξυνασχαλεΐ [he is distressed together] for ξυνασχαλᾷ [he is distressed together] at lines 161 and 243; see him in the Thesaurus under ἀσχαλάω [to be distressed].
he marries such a marriage, in which he was once secure.

It is a Sicilian word (for σύαγρός [wild boar]), whose use Athenaeus 9 p. 402 explains by the fact that Aeschylus, having stayed long in Sicily, πολλαῖς κέχρηται φωναῖς Σικελικαῖς [used many Sicilian words].
and he went into the cave like a wild boar
where Asopus waters the plain with his streams
leaping over the plain of Asopus
he eats food that is destructive, as you see, to his race
(with the verse supplied by me) as in Sophocles OC 1322 Parthenopaeus is called πιστὸς Αταλάντης γόνος [faithful son of Atalanta].
Parthenopaeus the Arcadian, son of Atalanta,
but do not toil at all
but he rages with a feeble trick
but tell me this, turning back again
